title: The Guru bows to the disciple
hook: Bhai Gurdas marvels that Nanak bowed to Angad, making the disciple the Guru (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Multan: a full cup, and a jasmine flower that spilled nothing. Today, a handover that runs the other way.

A handover at work tends to go one way. The old boss signs the papers, gives a short speech, maybe cuts a cake, and walks out the door, and the new one is still, somehow, the junior. Near the end of his first var, Bhai Gurdas tells a handover that runs the other way round. Baba Nanak chooses the one who will carry the light after him, and then does something that makes Bhai Gurdas marvel. Today: Angad.
screen: `A HANDOVER, THE USUAL WAY.` → `BABA NANAK CHOOSES WHO COMES NEXT.` → `A HANDOVER THE OTHER WAY ROUND.`

segments.voice: The disciple's name was Lehna. Bhai Gurdas says that while Nanak was still living, he set Lehna in the Guru's place and had the canopy held over his head, the sign of the Guru's seat. He gave him a new name, Angad. And Bhai Gurdas treats it as a wonder: the master bowing to the one he'd chosen. The bow is sung in the Guru Granth Sahib too, in the var of Satta and Balwand on Ang nine hundred sixty-six: the Guru bowed to the disciple while Nanak was still alive. Bhai Gurdas pictures it as light merging into light. Nanak's light didn't go out. It wasn't handed along like a lamp passed from one hand to another, leaving the first hand empty. It merged: the same light, now in a new form. Sikhs often sum it up in a phrase that turns the order upside down: the Guru became the disciple, and the disciple became the Guru. In Sikh teaching, Guruship isn't a possession to clutch until the end. It's a light, and the one who carries it is the first to bow to it when it shines in someone else. Bhai Gurdas goes on to tell the next handings on in the same spirit, and the pattern carries into Sikh life now, where Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru. Bowing to someone you taught means trusting that what you gave them is theirs now, and might grow in their hands in ways it never could in yours. Nanak, in Bhai Gurdas's telling, does it with the Guru's own seat.
screen: `LEHNA IN THE GURU'S SEAT.` · `NANAK BOWS TO HIM.` · `LIGHT MERGING INTO LIGHT.` · `GURU BECOMES DISCIPLE, DISCIPLE GURU.` · then, large: `THE TEACHER BOWS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone younger who knows something you don't: a niece who knows the app, a new colleague who sees an old problem fresh, a teenager who once corrected you and turned out to be right. Picture asking them, simply, show me, and notice whatever in you resists that, and let it soften a little. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with that person in mind.
Angad, the name Nanak gave Lehna when he placed him in the Guru's seat and bowed to him: the Guru became the disciple, and the disciple became the Guru.
Your line: the teacher bows. The light stayed whole as it moved. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's handing on to Guru Angad, as Bhai Gurdas tells it, as one light passing into a new form, and today bow before the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru.

chat.says: How did Guru Nanak hand on the Guru's seat? Did he just name a successor?
options: He set Lehna in the Guru's seat, renamed him Angad, and bowed to him: light into light.
He named his own son, since the Guru's seat passed down the family line.
He waited until he died, and the Sikhs then voted on who should follow him.
chat.meaning: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak, while living, installed Lehna as Angad and bowed to him; Satta and Balwand sing the same bow on Ang 966.

notes: Var 1 pauri 45 paraphrased from memory: while living, Baba installs Lehna, waves the canopy over him, names him Angad, bows to him; 'jot samani jot vich'; Guru becomes disciple and disciple Guru. Confirm the pauri number and that the 'Guru became disciple' phrasing belongs to this pauri (it is often cited from Bhai Gurdas and from later writings).
'Bhai Gurdas goes on to tell the next handings on in the same spirit' assumes Var 1 pauris 46–48 describe the later successions this way; confirm.
No age claim is made: the practice 'learn from someone younger' comes from the outline, not from any claim about Angad's age.
Gurmukhi ਜੋਤਿ: confirm the transliteration 'joht' for the original game.

Audit (2026-10-01): the bow and the 'Guru became disciple, disciple Guru' phrase were attributed directly to Bhai Gurdas; the phrase is now 'Sikhs often sum it up', and the bow is also sourced to Satta and Balwand, Ang 966 ('gur chele rahras keeyee Nanak salamat theevadai'). 'Canopy waved' changed to 'held' (the chhatar is held; the chaur is waved). Keeper: confirm Var 1 pauri 45 has Nanak's bow and 'acharje acharj' (wonder).
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
